title: A Desert Plant That Cools Itself by 'Sweating'
summary:
Death Valley in California is one of the hottest places on Earth. In summer, it is often hotter than 49 degrees Celsius (120 degrees Fahrenheit). But a shrub called the Arizona honeysweet grows well there.

Scientists at Michigan State University found its secret. The plant lets out water vapor through tiny holes on its leaves and stems. This is called transpiration, and it works a lot like sweating.

The scientists grew more than 1,200 young plants in a lab. Then they slowly made it hotter, up to 60 degrees C (140 degrees F). Some leaves stayed about 13 degrees C (23 degrees F) cooler than the air. When the scientists closed the tiny holes, the plants did not live as long.

"This cooling makes the difference between life and death," said scientist Seung Yon Rhee.

Not every plant survived. Rhee thinks their DNA may explain why some lasted longer. The findings have not yet been checked by other scientists.
why_it_matters: Just like you sweat to cool down on a hot day, plants have their own ways to beat the heat.

background_read: Plants take in water through their roots and let some of it out through tiny holes in their leaves.
When water leaves a plant as vapor, it helps cool the plant, a lot like sweat cools your skin.
Death Valley is a very hot, dry desert, so plants there need special tricks to survive.
